explanations: Diamond is carbon in a cubic crystal, the hardest natural material, formed deep in the mantle and carried up by volcanic eruptions.
Graphite is the most stable form of carbon under standard conditions, used above all in refractories and lithium-ion batteries.
Graphene is a single sheet of carbon hexagons one atom thick, isolated in 2004 in Manchester with graphite and adhesive tape.
Diamond, graphite and graphene are all allotropes of carbon: the same element, arranged three different ways.

sources.excerpt: Diamond is a mineral form of the element carbon with its atoms arranged in a crystal structure called diamond cubic.
Diamond has the highest hardness and thermal conductivity of any natural material, properties that are used in major industrial applications such as cutting and polishing tools.
Most were formed at depths between 150 and 250 kilometres (93 and 155 mi) in the Earth's mantle, although a few have come from as deep as 800 kilometres (500 mi).
Much more recently (hundreds to tens of million years ago), they were carried to the surface in volcanic eruptions and deposited in igneous rocks known as kimberlites and lamproites.
Graphite occurs naturally and is the most stable form of carbon under standard conditions.

Synthetic and natural graphite are consumed on a large scale (1.3 million metric tons per year in 2022) for uses in many critical industries including refractories (50%), lithium-ion batteries (18%), foundries (10%), and lubricants (5%), among others (17%).
In graphene, the carbon forms a sheet of interlocked atoms as hexagons one carbon atom thick. The result resembles the face of a honeycomb.
In 2004, the material was isolated and characterized by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at the University of Manchester using a piece of graphite and adhesive tape.
Carbon is capable of forming many allotropes (structurally different forms of the same element) due to its valency (tetravalent). Well-known forms of carbon include diamond and graphite.
